title: Catholic: the Mass
hook: Catholics believe Christ is truly present in the bread and wine

segments.voice: Yesterday: Christmas, the baby in the manger. Your line was a child in the cold. Did your small gift reach someone? Day two hundred sixty, and a new visit: the Catholic tradition.

Walk into almost any Catholic church on a weekday afternoon. It's quiet. A few people sit scattered in the pews, not talking, not reading, just there. Near the front, beside a small locked box, a candle is burning in red glass. It burns day and night. If you asked one of the people sitting there why they came, many would point to that box and say, simply: because he's here. Today, on our visit to the Catholic tradition, we start at the center: the Eucharist, and what Catholics call the real presence.
screen: `A QUIET CHURCH, A WEEKDAY.` → `A RED CANDLE THAT NEVER GOES OUT.` → `BECAUSE HE'S HERE.`

segments.voice: Eucharist is a Greek word: thanksgiving. It's kin to charis, grace, from a few days ago. It names the meal at the heart of the Mass, which goes back to the night before Jesus died. At a Passover-season supper with his disciples, he took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them. In the Douay-Rheims translation: "Take ye, and eat. This is my body." Then the cup: his blood of the covenant. And, in Luke's telling, do this in memory of me. Catholics take those words at their plainest. They believe that at Mass, when the priest says Jesus' words over the bread and wine, they become the body and blood of Christ: still looking and tasting like bread and wine, but truly him. The Church's word for this, from the Middle Ages, is transubstantiation, a change in what the thing most deeply is. That's why it's called the real presence. And that's what the little box, the tabernacle, holds: consecrated bread kept after Mass, for the sick and for prayer. The red lamp says someone is home. Christians understand this meal differently, and it's worth saying who says what. Orthodox Christians also believe Christ is truly present, and prefer to call it a holy mystery rather than define how. Lutherans speak of a real presence too, in their own terms. Many other Protestants see the meal as a powerful remembrance and sign. For Catholics, the Mass is the source and summit of the whole Christian life, and a quiet church is never really empty.
screen: `EUCHARIST — THANKSGIVING.` · `TAKE YE, AND EAT. THIS IS MY BODY.` · `THE TABERNACLE AND THE RED LAMP.` · `WHO SAYS WHAT ABOUT THE MEAL.` · then, large: `REAL PRESENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you like, and if one is near, you can sit in a quiet church sometime this week; the doors of many are open by day. For now, sit wherever you are and practice presence the simple way. Notice what is really here: your breath, the weight of your body, the sounds in the room. No need to add anything. Just be present to what's present. The bell holds the time.
Eucharist. Thanksgiving: the meal of the Mass, where Catholics believe Christ is truly present in the bread and wine. Today's word.
Your line: real presence. Today, give one person your real presence: phone down, eyes up, listening all the way. Day two hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Catholics attend Mass every Sunday, and many daily, receiving Communion; many also pray quietly before the tabernacle, where a sanctuary lamp burns to show the consecrated bread is kept there.
